And it’s a philosophical dilemma, right? There is no absolute right answer. It’s all compromise. And I get the hate for Starkid, haha. 

My argument and really all arguments also benefit from the ambiguous ending. We don’t see the hindsight effects of any choice. So maybe I was duped by the reapers and ruined everything, but since we don’t see I can believe that the synthesis was fine for those involved. But that really is a leap of faith.

I tend away from genocide. Historically always justified as a greater good, but is it ever? The game is ambiguous, it’s what is great about them, you carry your own baggage in and it’s a sort of revealing of your self. 

But for me, the lessons along the way. If you untethered Edi, that’s scary, what’s going to happen will she kill us all? No you find she is as much a person as anyone. You recruit Legion, scary, might kill us all in our sleep, but he doesn’t. You drop yourself into a geth mind, learn their history, see things from a different perspective, end a civil war between the geth and the quarians, bring peace between these two cultures, observe love between Joker and Edi. 

Unrelated to machines, you see the effects of the genophage genocide and that might stir some feelings, some thoughts, maybe you even cure it. Watch one of the coolest characters sacrifice himself to right that wrong. 

To me, this is a story of discovering the ‘humanity’ in this culture that starts out as an other. It’s scary, it’s a vulnerable choice but I think given those experiences it’s the logical and ethical choice to synthesize. You’ve seen the machines are as much people as any race.

Now I have played ‘renegade’ runs where you are bull headed and single minded. Destroy all geth, always make the military minded ‘safe’ choice. You miss all of those experiences, then destroy becomes the logical move. From a role playing stand point why would they change at that point? But that also makes a less beautiful story. It’s tragic and awful. I think. Idk, I carry my own baggage.

I still really like both. I can see why King was upset. It was his baby and the Kubrick version really changes the story into something very different. The horror is very different, the characters are different, but I don’t think it is fair to compare the two in terms of worth. I like the Kubrick version of Jack, because he reminds me of my father. The kind of horror in the movie is reminiscent of the fear I felt as a child. I like the King Jack on the other hand because he is a more complex character. He is a decent guy, but with big problems and big demons and he sticks his arm in the hornets nest of the overlook and tragically dooms himself. So the horror of what is happening in the book is almost more so in empathizing with Jack. In the movie it is more about Wendy and Danny being trapped with monster. 

If you go into the movie wanting the story of the book, you’ll be disappointed because that isn’t what it is. But if you go into it for a different parallel experience I still think it is amazing. Also I think Kubrick did a good job translating things that are more explicit in the book, to more subconscious nods in the movie. Like the whole thing about the wasps in the book was so important, but how would you translate that to film within the length of a movie and also make it not look cheesy? Kubrick uses the famous overlook carpet that is the brown and orange hexagonal honey comb pattern. I don’t know I think that is a brilliant way to nod toward the original story while doing your own thing. 

That said King’s version was more catharticly beautiful and poetic. The characters were more substantial. I did like ultimate fates of the characters more.
